evidence: Hor. C. 2.19.4: aurīs capripedum Satyrōrum acūtās
terms.comment: Sharpened, and so pointed or sharp: of ears, a nose, a peak, a blade. “To a point” is in acūtum (Livy, Curtius).

terms.gloss: sharpened to a point at the end
evidence: Caes. B.G. 4.17: tigna bīna sēsquipedālia paulum ab īmō praeacūta
Cato Agr. 40: sūrculus āridus praeacūtus (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Of a stake, a peg, or a pencil sharpened at one end.

evidence: Liv. 37.27: in acūtum cacūmen ā fundō satis lātō fastīgātus

terms.gloss: pointed, ending in a sharp point
terms.comment: Pliny’s word, of leaves and snouts, from mūcrō, a sword’s point (see “point”).

phrases.latin: Aspice aurēs fēlis: quam acūtae sunt!
phrases.english: Look at the cat’s ears: how pointy they are!
Draw a pointy nose, like a fox’s.

phrases.latin: Bacchum in remōtīs carmina rūpibus vīdī docentem, crēdite posterī, Nymphāsque discentīs et aurīs capripedum Satyrōrum acūtās
phrases.english: I saw Bacchus on far-off rocks teaching songs (believe me, you who come after), and the Nymphs learning them, and the pointed ears of the goat-footed Satyrs

phrases.latin: ipse collis est in modum mētae in acūtum cacūmen ā fundō satis lātō fastīgātus
phrases.english: the hill itself is like a cone, rising from a fairly broad base to a sharp peak

sources: Lewis & Short: acuo · Lewis & Short: praeacuo · Lewis & Short: fastigo · Lewis & Short: mucronatus
Morgan–Owens, Adumbratio: s.v. pointed.
